items.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
items.headline: Looping early layers inside each denoising step lets uniform diffusion LMs match a ~0.5T-token baseline's NLL with up to 3.3x fewer FLOPs
items.summary: Uniform diffusion LMs (UDLMs) corrupt tokens to other vocabulary tokens rather than to a mask, so the model must denoise from a context that may itself be wrong. That makes them costlier to train than masked diffusion LMs, though they are reported to reason better. The authors take selective looping (re-applying a few early Transformer layers several times within each denoising step), previously shown to help masked diffusion LMs at iso-FLOPs, and apply it to UDLMs without changing the training objective or the sampler. They also study the distribution from which the loop count is sampled during training.
items.result: Per the abstract: looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of a non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5T tokens with up to 2.8x fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and up to 3.3x fewer on FineWeb-Edu. At matched function evaluations, generation perplexity is up to 9.8% lower than the non-looped model, with most of the gain at moderate loop counts. Sampling small loop counts more often in training uses 12% fewer loops on downstream tasks than uniform loop-count sampling, at equal accuracy.
items.critique: Read from the abstract only; the paper body could not be fetched, so model sizes, compute accounting and the downstream task list are unchecked. Results are 'up to' figures. The baseline is a non-looped UDLM; there is no comparison here with a masked diffusion LM or an autoregressive model at equal FLOPs, so the gap UDLMs must close is not quantified. Generation perplexity is measured by an external scorer and can reward low-diversity text. Looping cuts parameters, not inference compute per step, so wall-clock cost is not reported. No code link on the arXiv page.

items.title: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models
items.headline: 4-bit n-gram embedding tables cut table memory ~75% and keep >99% of their loss gain; 47-55% savings on two large MoEs
items.summary: Several open-weight LLMs now add n-gram embedding tables (learned vectors for 2- and 3-token sequences, looked up at inference); the abstract cites 196B parameters in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's Engram memory. The authors store these tables at low precision, compare quantization methods and per-table bit allocations, test brief fine-tuning to recover losses at very low bit widths, and try reinvesting the freed memory in larger tables.
items.result: Per the abstract: in nanochat-, Llama- and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, 4-bit tables cut table memory by about 75% while keeping over 99% of the validation-loss improvement the tables provide; larger tables at low bit width can beat the original full-precision tables while using less memory. Applied post hoc to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables reduce table memory by 47-55% with under 1.2% perplexity increase and largely retained downstream accuracy.
items.critique: Read from the abstract only. From-scratch experiments are on small model families, and 'largely retained' downstream performance on the large models is not quantified in the abstract. The 47-55% figure is less than the 75% at 4 bits, suggesting mixed or higher precision on the big models, which the abstract does not explain. Lookup tables are memory-bound but cheap in compute, so savings in memory footprint may not translate into speed; no latency or throughput numbers. Closely overlaps 'N-Gram Memories at Two Bits' (2610.21810, covered 21 Oct); the abstract does not compare against it.

items.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
items.headline: KV-Surgeon compacts a fixed context's KV cache offline with a quadratic surrogate; up to +4 QA points over attention matching at 50x
items.summary: Offline KV compaction builds a smaller cache for a fixed long context once and reuses it across many queries. Existing methods score each entry independently, but softmax renormalization couples deletions. KV-Surgeon fits a quadratic surrogate of the attention-output error on calibration queries, greedily deletes entries using its closed-form solution, updates the remaining entries in closed form after each deletion to compensate, and finally refits the retained keys' logit biases and values. A faster variant is also given. Code (MIT) is at github.com/ZIB-IOL/KV-Surgeon and supports Qwen3/Qwen3-MoE, Llama 3.1 and Gemma 3.
items.result: Per the abstract: on QuALITY, LongHealth and Long Code Arena, it improves the cost-accuracy trade-off at every compaction ratio tested for dense and MoE models from 4B to 30B. At 50x compaction it gains up to 4 QA accuracy points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026) at comparable cost; the fast variant also beats it at two-fifths of the cost.
items.critique: Numbers come from the abstract; per-benchmark tables were not read. 'Up to 4 points' is a best case. Only applies to fixed contexts queried repeatedly, and depends on calibration queries resembling real ones; robustness to query distribution shift is not stated in the abstract. Compaction cost is compared, but serving latency is not reported. Submitted 19 Oct; omitted from earlier digests because its page could not be read.

items.title: Drift Says When, Budget Says How Much: Rate-Controlled KV Re-selection for Long-Form Multimodal Generation
items.headline: RCR re-selects MLLM visual-token KV when attention drifts to evicted tokens; beats InfiniGen by 1.6-3.8 ROUGE-L in 5 of 6 settings
items.summary: Multimodal LLM KV compression usually picks which visual tokens to keep once at prefill. On long detailed captions attention moves across the image, so even an oracle one-shot selection agrees with the uncompressed output at only 0.44-0.52 ROUGE-L (32 tokens per head). Rate-Controlled Refresh (RCR) keeps a full prefix KV copy off the GPU cache and measures drift, the attention mass a step puts on evicted tokens, with a low-rank detector over 8 SVD-rotated key channels (about 4x smaller than InfiniGen's). When drift crosses a per-sample threshold, that layer re-selects tokens, scoring the detector's top 4c candidates exactly and keeping c. The threshold is adjusted multiplicatively so a target fraction (0.4) of layer-steps refresh, and decisions run on the GPU without host syncs.
items.result: At 64 prefix entries per head on Qwen2-VL-7B, LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B (TextCaps, DetailCaps): beats InfiniGen in 5 of 6 model-task settings by +1.6 to +3.8 ROUGE-L (e.g. Qwen2-VL DetailCaps .598 vs .570; LLaVA-NeXT DetailCaps .485 vs .451), and stays within 1.7 points of exact per-step re-selection while refreshing 40-48% of layer-steps. Beats random timing at the same rate by 5.0 points and periodic 50% refresh by 2.0 on Qwen2-VL. Traffic is 63-77 vectors per step and head vs InfiniGen's 64. The margin shrinks to +2.7 at 128 entries and +1.2 (not significant) at 256.
items.critique: Fidelity is ROUGE-L against the uncompressed model's output, not correctness, and there is no human evaluation. Only 7-8B models, captioning and one 300-video task; on video it does not beat a fixed-threshold rule and is not significantly better than InfiniGen on Qwen2-VL. Baselines are the authors' re-implementations in a shared simulation that keeps the full prefix on the GPU, so costs are traffic estimates; no measured latency in a real offloading system. Components were tuned on a 100-image dev split without multiple-comparison correction (all stated by the authors).

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB
items.headline: NVIDIA releases Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: Gemma-4-E4B-it post-trained with RL, shipped as Q4_K_M with a DFlash speculative drafter
items.summary: Open model released 23 Oct 2026 (HF and build.nvidia.com). It is Google's Gemma-4-E4B-it (8B total, ~4B effective parameters, Gemma 4 architecture) further post-trained by NVIDIA with RL (GRPO per the card; RLVR and RLHF via NeMo-RL/NeMo-Gym per NVIDIA's research page) for tool calling, instruction following and instruction hierarchy. NVIDIA's research page says the BF16 checkpoint was quantized to Q4_K_M with llama.cpp using importance-matrix calibration, targeting about 4GB of memory; context is 64K. A separate DFlash drafter (NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash) proposes all draft tokens in one forward pass for speculative decoding. License OpenMDW-1.1.
items.result: Model card (Q4_K_M, NeMo Gym harness) vs Gemma-4-E4B-it / Qwen3.5-4B / Nemotron-3-Nano-4B: MultiChallenge 55.60 vs 39.36 / 52.23 / 34.53; IHEval 82.40 vs 66.61 / 62.87 / 53.75; BFCL-v3 67.31 vs 65.03 / 70.56 / 59.07; Tau2-Bench 52.32 vs 38.72 / 61.74 / 14.89; RULER 64K 85.76 vs 86.14 / 95.37 / 91.31. NVIDIA's research page reports 133.4 tok/s decode and 548 ms TTFT on an RTX 5070 using 3.5GB VRAM, and 15.5 tok/s on Jetson Orin Nano (Q4_K_M, batch 1, llama.cpp CUDA), and says DFlash gives up to 21% more throughput than Gemma 4 E4B's original MTP drafter.
items.critique: All numbers are vendor-reported in NVIDIA's own harness. The model card and the research page give different scores for the same benchmarks (e.g. MultiChallenge 55.60 vs 53.1, BFCL-v3 67.31 vs 68.5) without explaining the setting difference. It trails Qwen3.5-4B on Tau2-Bench, BFCL-v3, IFBench and long-context RULER, and is below its own Gemma base on RULER. 'E4B' is 8B total parameters; the 4GB footprint comes from standard Q4_K_M quantization, not a new compression method. The speed table and the DFlash speedup come from the research page, not the card, and there is no head-to-head speed comparison against the base model at equal quantization.

items.title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14's Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
items.headline: AWS and i14 detail training and serving Laplace 3B, a pure gated-linear-attention model with a fixed 29.5 MB state, on Trainium2
items.summary: Laplace 3B (3.028B parameters) replaces softmax attention in all 24 layers with Simple Gated Linear Attention, using fixed per-head geometric decay (half-lives from 1 to ~2,048 tokens), a width-4 causal depthwise conv, and a SiLU GLU FFN. Its recurrent state is 29.5 MB per sequence regardless of context length. It is trained on one trn2.48xlarge (16 Trainium2 chips) in native PyTorch via TorchNeuron with FSDP2 and distributed Muon, toward 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens. Switching Muon's communication from gather/broadcast to all_to_all cut per-rank traffic from 10.87 GB to 0.45 GB per step. Serving uses an unmodified vLLM engine with a wrapper and a compiled decode step. Published 20 Oct 2026.
items.result: Training throughput rose from 73,378 to 119,934 tokens/s (1.63x) after the Muon all_to_all change, with a loss curve the post calls bit-identical; training had reached step 84,210 (~44B tokens, loss ~2.37) at writing. Serving: 11,544 output tokens/s across 1,280 concurrent sequences on one trn2.48xlarge; compiling decode gave 1.7x over eager. Growing the prompt from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens added 0.5% to cost per output token. The post claims the state is ~82x smaller than an 8,192-token KV cache.
items.critique: Vendor post co-written with i14. No quality benchmarks of any kind, including long-context retrieval where pure linear attention is known to be weak, and no transformer baseline at equal size or tokens. Training was less than half done. The 82x KV comparison does not say which transformer configuration it assumes. No dollar cost figures, and the claim that Trainium beat the original GPU Triton kernel has no numbers. Recompilation for new batch shapes took 47.5% of decode time in one test.

items.title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation
items.headline: AOPD weights each teacher action in on-policy distillation by its estimated advantage for the student, using only standard student rollouts
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains the student on its own trajectories but assumes it should imitate the teacher at every step. AOPD separates what the teacher prefers from what helps the student succeed: each teacher action is weighted by its counterfactual advantage for the student, reinforcing helpful actions and downweighting unhelpful ones. Computing that advantage exactly would need extra rollouts; the authors show the objective can be estimated from ordinary student rollouts and their final rewards using teacher importance weights on sampled actions, keeping OPD's rollout cost.
items.result: The abstract reports gains over distillation and RL baselines on math, coding and MedQA, in both external-teacher and self-distillation settings, but gives no numbers; the paper body could not be read in this run.
items.critique: No quantitative result could be verified, and model sizes, baselines and compute are unknown from the abstract. Importance weighting between teacher and student policies can have high variance when they diverge, and the abstract does not say how this is controlled. Similar advantage-shaped OPD variants have appeared in recent months (e.g. OPD+, SAF-OPD); whether they are compared is unknown. Needs a reward signal, so it does not apply to reward-free distillation.

items.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
items.headline: CausalCoT splits a problem into a DAG of sub-questions and lets each node attend only to its parents, aiming for more faithful CoT
items.summary: With dense attention, a model can read the answer off the context directly, so chain-of-thought steps may be post-hoc rationalizations. CausalCoT is an inference-time framework that decomposes a problem into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions and evaluates each node using only its direct causal parents as context, removing attention to unrelated content. The graph also allows test-time interventions on a node whose corrections propagate downstream.
items.result: Per the abstract: competitive accuracy on several reasoning benchmarks, with explanation faithfulness and causal sensitivity of intermediate steps improved by 12 points on average and up to 21 points over the strongest baseline.
items.critique: Abstract only; benchmarks, models and the faithfulness metric are not specified there, and 'competitive' accuracy suggests no accuracy gain. Faithfulness metrics are defined by the authors' own interventions, which the method is built to respond to. Running one call per DAG node with isolated contexts likely increases inference cost and latency, which the abstract does not report. Included as an off-focus item on inference-time structure.
